# Bootstrapping an AI-Native Ecosystem {#sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem}

![](images/ch12-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="One team can improve records and comparisons now, while cross-team, physical or silicon, and public-program claims require different shared infrastructure."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "The more designers involved in using the new methods, and the better they are able to communicate with each other, the faster the process of cultural integration runs."
>
> — Lynn Conway, *The MPC Adventures* (1981) [@Conway1981MPCAdventures, p. 2]
:::

An architecture team can retain failed runs, measure its costs, and improve its comparisons without waiting for the discipline to agree on a standard. It cannot make another team's tool interpret a record correctly, establish a neutral public benchmark, or provide its own access to a fabrication process through better recordkeeping alone. Those limits require coordination. This chapter separates local practices from proposals for shared interfaces, implementation access, evaluation, and education. The proposals connect limits encountered earlier in the book to work the community could undertake; their adoption and effectiveness remain to be established.

## Ecosystem Workstreams and Dependencies {#sec-staging-sequence}

In the late 1970s, Mead and Conway connected structured VLSI abstractions to fabrication access through the ARPANET-enabled MPC79 run [@MeadConway1980VLSI; @Conway1981MPCAdventures]. Shared wafer services such as MOSIS subsequently gave university teams a path from a design to a die [@MOSIS1981VLSI]. A shared representation becomes more useful when researchers can also reach the implementation process needed to test it. Architecture 2.0 needs a modern counterpart that connects exchangeable study records, comparable evaluations, and access to physical implementation. The ownership boundaries of @sec-what-architect-owns remain in force, but some of the evidence an owner needs depends on infrastructure beyond the organization.

Deploying closed-loop search without shared interfaces risks compounding fragmentation in electronic design automation (EDA). A learned placer may depend on features specific to a tool version, standard-cell library, or process deck. Within that environment, the dependency can remain implicit; transferring the method exposes it. The operational layers of @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration describe the scope of automated work, but none guarantees interoperability. A system that must carry a design across tools and organizations also needs explicit agreements about those dependencies.

Six proposals address different parts of that coordination problem. For each one, @tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence separates what a team can start inside its own repositories from what requires shared infrastructure, and identifies the earlier limit or risk that motivates the proposal.

| **Proposal** | **Ecosystem action** | **Local starting point** | **Coordination dependency** | **Earlier limit or risk** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Shared data schemas and tool contracts | Retain decision context, artifact identities, commands, returns, failures, and costs in a versioned record. | Cross-team comparison needs common semantics for identities, status, units, and tool results. | Tool-specific wrappers and limits on model transfer across tool flows (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack). |
| 2 | Open implementation paths and cloud silicon shuttles | Exercise an open flow at a named manufacturable or predictive node and state the resulting evidence boundary. | Silicon claims need a manufacturable process design kit (PDK), an accepted fabrication path, and device measurements; commercial-node signoff needs foundry-qualified decks, libraries, tools, and access. | Physical timing, power-delivery, and thermal checks left unmeasured (@sec-what-architect-owns). |
| 3 | Consortium governance and matched benchmarks | Run a matched local comparison with pinned tasks, checks, budgets, and total-cost accounting. | A public leaderboard needs neutral rules, shared task versions, audit capacity, and comparator governance. | Benchmark-health and matched-baseline risks (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). |
| 4 | Grand challenges and architecture contests | Run a narrow evaluator-owned challenge with a credible baseline and explicit untested conditions. | Cross-organization contests depend on stable interfaces, comparable checks, and enforceable resource accounting. | None in this book. |
| 5 | Public repositories of failed attempts | Retain failed, invalid, timed-out, and rejected attempts alongside successful runs. | Shared repositories need schemas, privacy and licensing rules, stewardship, and controls against misleading or unsafe data. | Censored and purged failed runs (@sec-data-representations-world-models). |
| 6 | University curricula and workflow review | Teach failure diagnosis, evidence qualification, matched comparison, and authority boundaries now. | A badge also needs published criteria, trained reviewers, appeals, maintenance, and evidence that the badge predicts the claimed practice. | None as a recorded stop; @sec-what-architect-owns names the apprenticeship gap as a risk. |
: **Local adoption can proceed in parallel; shared claims create dependencies.** The proposals identify work that can begin now and the infrastructure required before a team makes broader cross-organizational, silicon, or certification claims. This is a dependency map, not a program that has been run. {#tbl-ecosystem-staging-sequence tbl-colwidths="[6,18,25,26,25]"}

Grand challenges and workflow badges are proposals for organizing shared research and review, rather than remedies tested in the book's worked studies. A contest could focus several groups on one unresolved problem; a badge could make the scope of a workflow review explicit. The chapter treats these two proposals as sketches whose value would need to be tested. The other four respond directly to limits encountered in the preceding chapters.

The local starting points still consume resources. Tool logs may already contain wall-clock time and accelerator hours, but license use and human triage time can require additional collection. Retaining failed runs needs storage and enough context to interpret them later. A matched baseline also spends evaluation budget. These are costs a team can plan and control; agreement on what another organization will accept is a different dependency. That distinction lets a student or a small laboratory begin a useful study without claiming that the shared infrastructure already exists.

The proposals group into four workstreams in @fig-ecosystem-roadmap. Open foundations connect tool interfaces to accessible implementation paths. Governance defines how results will be compared and disputed. Evaluation puts those rules to work in shared studies and contests. Skills and review prepare people to diagnose the resulting artifacts. These workstreams can develop concurrently, but they need to exchange records and requirements: a benchmark, for example, cannot demand a physical check that participating laboratories have no path to run.

![**Ecosystem workstreams share dependencies without imposing a universal adoption order.** Open foundations, governance, evaluation, and skills and review exchange records and requirements. Horizontal connectors show coordination needed for cross-team claims, while local practices within every workstream begin independently. Negative design attempts feed back into schemas, checks, and surrogate calibration.](images/fig-ecosystem-roadmap){#fig-ecosystem-roadmap width="80%" fig-alt="Four coordinating workstreams show open foundations, governance, evaluation, and skills and review. Actions cover schemas, physical-design paths, matched benchmarks, contests, failure repositories, curricula, and review. Dashed connectors indicate shared dependencies rather than a universal adoption sequence, and a feedback arrow returns negative attempts to the foundations."}

The defining mechanism in @fig-ecosystem-roadmap is the feedback loop returning negative design attempts to the shared foundations. Records of unroutable placements, negative timing slack, and Unified Power Format (UPF) domain violations can expose missing schema fields, benchmark constraints, or property checks and provide data for surrogate calibration. Horizontal connectors represent dependencies for cross-organizational claims, not preconditions for local exploration. Whether this coordination model scales across the semiconductor ecosystem remains an open question.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Anchor AI-Native Design Tools in Open Foundations"}
**The principle:** Develop shared interfaces, reference paths, and comparison practices around the checks that independent teams need to perform. Open schemas, accessible implementation flows, neutral benchmarks, and qualified failure repositories are proposed ways to make that work possible.

**The application:** Begin local cost, provenance, failure-retention, and comparison practices now. Require shared contracts for cross-team comparability. Support physical claims with a qualified implementation path and silicon claims with retained measurements from fabricated devices. A certification claim must state the scope actually reviewed.
:::

## Shared Data Schemas and Tool Contracts {#sec-standardized-data-lineage}

Consider what happens when a retained study record reaches another team's tool flow. A timing slack value is useful only if the receiving tool knows its units, corner, and constraint status. When an optimizer exchanges spatial coordinates or power-domain declarations through ad hoc strings, a parser can accept the input while assigning it the wrong meaning. A surrogate might interpret an unconstrained clock port as a zero-delay wire, or infer that an unrouted power rail has zero resistance. The transfer problem of @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack therefore begins before a model makes a prediction: the organizations must agree on what the exchanged state means.

Just as Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1666 (SystemC) established common modeling semantics across commercial and open environments [@IEEE2011SystemC1666], a standards consortium (such as MLCommons[^fn-mlcommons-c12] or CHIPS Alliance) could standardize tool and record interfaces before proprietary silos lock in competing application programming interfaces (APIs). Open schema contracts would let generators, surrogate models, and verification engines interact through stable, machine-readable specifications. The proposed Open Agentic Interface (OAI) would formalize this coordination through three record schemas (@fig-oai-schemas).

- **Design problem formulations.** Explicit declarations of permitted design changes, locked constraints, evaluation checks, and acceptance criteria ($s_{\text{design}}$). The prospective Lighthouse cache study of @sec-architecture-20-ontology declares one swept parameter, `l2.capacity` at 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB, against fixed cache policies and interfaces, with bank count and static random-access memory (SRAM) macro organization to be derived from capacity under a declared rule. The separate executed array study of @sec-running-the-loop declares processing element (PE) geometries bounded at 1,024 elements with a mandatory 32 by 32 baseline. A shared schema must preserve their different status and scope. Lighthouse's 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope and 8.33\ ms frame deadline are prospective system obligations; the array study's simulator returns do not establish compliance with them. The formulation must also identify the technology target, distinguishing a predictive PDK such as ASAP7 from commercial signoff on a node such as TSMC N3E. When a generator proposes a different hardware or software organization, the formulation must describe the changed interfaces and obligations so the receiving team can determine which earlier checks still apply.
- **Lineage headers.** Declarations of candidate artifacts, parent inputs, transformations, tool flags, structural representations, and environment configurations ($s_{\text{env}}$). A cryptographic hash identifies exact bytes; a Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) attestation binds an issuer to a declaration [@SLSA2026Framework].[^fn-slsa-attestation-c12] Neither mechanism proves semantic correctness, and an attestation remains only as trustworthy as its builder, signing key, and storage path. Lineage headers track the exact inputs and environments used to generate an artifact, such as a SystemC memory controller or a high-level synthesis kernel (@sec-data-representations-world-models). Rather than relying on informal logs, these headers retain structured records of prompt and commit hashes, intermediate representations (IR) (like abstract syntax trees (ASTs), control-data flow graphs (CDFGs), and Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) / Circuit IR Compilers and Tools (CIRCT)), execution seeds, and environment definitions (container digests and CLI arguments). A team might export structural hashes, compiler pass fingerprints, and bounding-box geometry metrics while withholding internal transistor topologies, unreleased instruction set architecture (ISA) opcodes, and proprietary foundry cell libraries. Those summaries still require disclosure review, including an assessment of what several records reveal together.
- **Multi-fidelity environmental contracts and tool AI-readiness assessment.** Typed input prerequisites, output schemas, declared error assumptions, status semantics, and property-appropriate checks across analytical models, cycle-level simulators, and register-transfer level (RTL) tools. Assessments verify whether tools such as gem5, Verilator, SCALE-Sim, Ramulator, OpenROAD, Yosys, and OpenSTA expose pinned container interfaces, structured state exports, checkpoint behavior, machine-parsable failures, and documented checks (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) state properties that bounded model checking (BMC) can check within a declared execution bound and under stated assumptions.[^fn-bmc-c12] A passing bounded check needs a separate completeness argument to establish the property for all executions of the model, and still cannot exclude a deadlock or other behavior the model omits.

![**The proposed Open Agentic Interface (OAI) would standardize three classes of record.** Design Problem Formulations declare search bounds and obligations; Attempt Lineage Headers identify artifacts and signed transformation declarations; Multi-Fidelity Environmental Contracts declare tool interfaces, assumptions, statuses, and checks. Together they support selective cross-organizational exchange, subject to separate access control, confidentiality, and trust policies.](images/fig-oai-schemas){#fig-oai-schemas width="80%" fig-alt="Diagram of three proposed Open Agentic Interface records: design problem formulation, attempt lineage header, and environmental contract. They capture bounds, artifact identities, transformation declarations, input prerequisites, error assumptions, and tool checks. A bottom box represents selective cross-organizational exchange subject to separate trust and confidentiality controls."}

Serialization is an implementation choice, not the contract. Protocol Buffers provide typed message definitions and cross-language serialization; the schema still has to specify units, missing values, and version compatibility. JSON-LD (a linked data format for JSON) lets a federated repository connect execution records to shared vocabularies through persistent identifiers. Neither format settles the meaning of a tool result. An OAI lineage header serializes the essential dependencies of a single transformation pass (@lst-ch12-lineage-header):

```{.protobuf #lst-ch12-lineage-header lst-cap="Example protobuf schema for capturing structural lineage dependencies"}
message LineageHeader {
  string run_id = 1;
  string parent_hash = 2;
  repeated string tool_flags = 3;
  string env_digest = 4;
  map<string, string> artifact_hashes = 5;
}
```

For example, a receiving tool could use the header to locate a timing report and verify that its bytes match the declared hash. Before consuming the report, it would also check the enclosing record's schema version, slack units, and status: a missing measurement must not become zero slack. If an attestation accompanies the record, a valid signature identifies the issuer of that declaration; it does not establish that the timing constraints were correct. The header supplies identity and dependencies, while the environmental contract supplies the rules for interpreting the return.

Where CIRCT and MLIR standardize the structural syntax of hardware modules and compiler dialects, OAI would carry the orchestration, lineage, and verification metadata governing how tools and generators manipulate those representations. It would also sit beside the interchange formats the industry already runs on, LEF/DEF for physical geometry, IEEE 1801 UPF for power intent, OpenAccess for design databases, and FIRRTL for generator output, carrying the record of how a run used those artifacts rather than replacing any of them. Each record class has a different preservation requirement. Problem formulations must retain their meaning after external parsing, lineage headers must remain interpretable apart from the original execution, and environmental contracts must make changes in tool behavior explicit when a tool is updated.

An interface proposal would become more useful if design teams required compatible exports from the tools they procure and contributed tests for how those exports are interpreted. That shared demand could reduce repeated wrapper work and let teams compare tool behavior on the same inputs. The consortium would still have to maintain compatibility tests as tools and schemas change.

[^fn-slsa-attestation-c12]: **SLSA Attestation**: A machine-readable, cryptographically signed metadata statement that records software supply-chain provenance, build environments, and transformation inputs [@SLSA2026Framework].

## The Precompetitive Open Infrastructure Imperative {#sec-precompetitive-infrastructure}

In deep-submicron and nanoscale fabrication, routing congestion, power-grid IR drop,[^fn-ir-drop-c12] UPF power-domain isolation, thermal dissipation, and manufacturability demand implementation evidence calibrated to the target node. Device structures, manufacturing rules, and interconnect resistance and capacitance vary with the process. Their effect on timing depends on the placed and routed design, so a nominal node label cannot establish that a candidate will close timing. Because commercial foundries protect their intellectual property behind strict nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), proprietary signoff tools, and qualified design-rule manuals, academic laboratories and early-stage startups face a structural barrier to physical design exploration.[^fn-pdk-lockin-c12]

Expanding open-source physical-design infrastructure and multi-project wafer (MPW) shuttle access narrows this structural divide. Open process design kits (PDKs), including SkyWater SKY130 (130\ nm CMOS) [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], IHP SG13G2 (130\ nm BiCMOS), and GlobalFoundries GF180MCU (180\ nm), expose models, libraries, and design rules for research on manufacturable processes. A manufacturable target process does not make every open PDK release production-qualified; fabrication requires a release and checks accepted by the chosen service [@IHPOpenPDK; @GlobalFoundriesGF180MCUOpenPDK]. Coupled with the open-source intermediate representation (IR) infrastructure of the CIRCT/Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) compiler ecosystem [@CIRCT] and open EDA engines (OpenROAD, Yosys, OpenSTA), open PDKs let researchers inspect and version more of the implementation flow. Reproducing a particular result still requires its inputs, tool versions, constraints, and execution record; open availability alone does not supply those dependencies.

The curated dependency illustration in @fig-ecosystem-network-graph shows how projects can share implementation components. It is a selected example, not an audited inventory of the ecosystem. A team using an established synthesis and layout flow can spend more of its effort on the candidate architecture and its constraints, while retaining the versions and checks of the reused components.

![**Selected projects illustrate reuse of shared implementation components.** This curated dependency graph connects open silicon projects with cores, tools, languages, and process support. Arrows represent selected project-to-dependency links; the force-directed layout illustrates their connections. The sample does not establish ecosystem-wide adoption or a historical transition toward a standard library.](images/plot_ch12.png){#fig-ecosystem-network-graph width="80%" fig-alt="Illustrative directed network of selected open silicon projects and their dependencies, including Yosys, Chisel, and OpenLane."}

The standard-library analogy concerns reuse, not inherited correctness. A generated macro still needs checks in its actual integration context, even if its toolchain and neighboring blocks have been exercised before. Shared dependencies make those checks easier to reproduce; they do not make every new composition pre-verified.

In academic research, ASAP7 serves as a predictive 7\ nm PDK for modeling scaling trends rather than manufacturable signoff [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7].[^fn-predictive-pdk-c12] It includes device models, design rules, and extraction decks, but its resulting designs are not manufacturable. Its modeled power, performance, and area (PPA) therefore cannot substitute for signoff against a commercial process's qualified decks. A candidate architecture that ranks highly under ASAP7 may fail timing or routing constraints when subjected to commercial foundry design rules. Correlating predictive-PDK evaluations with commercial TSMC N7, N3, or N2 characteristics constitutes a distinct research claim requiring matched industrial baselines, explicit parasitic derating models, and documented error bounds.

[^fn-predictive-pdk-c12]: **Predictive process design kit (PDK)**: An open, non-manufacturable cell library and technology model that abstracts geometric and electrical scaling trends for academic research without exposing proprietary foundry design rules or signoff decks [@ClarkEtAl2016ASAP7].

## Silicon Shuttles and Cost Reduction {#sec-silicon-shuttles}

Timing, power delivery, and thermal behavior can be analyzed before fabrication, but each analysis depends on its device models, parasitics, operating conditions, and package assumptions. A predictive kit supports claims within that modeled environment. Foundry-qualified analysis supports a different implementation claim, and empirical validation requires measurements on a fabricated die. The unmeasured checks in @sec-what-architect-owns therefore call for a named implementation or measurement path, not an undifferentiated demand for silicon. Shuttles address the final step by sharing fabrication costs among research designs, extending the MPC79 and MOSIS precedent [@Conway1981MPCAdventures; @MOSIS1981VLSI]. The cost comparison in @fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse explains why that access matters.

![**Fabrication access spans different processes and submission sizes.** (a) Compiled costs compare full-reticle masks, commercial MPW prototypes, and open-shuttle tiles. Mask-set values range from $\$35\ \text{thousand}$ ($2\ \mu\text{m}$) to $\$48\ \text{million}$ (3\ nm). The $\$460\ \text{thousand}$ prototype and $\$50$ open-process tile offer different capabilities, not a price reduction for the same chip. Shared fabrication follows MOSIS [@MOSIS1981VLSI]. (b) The Tiny Tapeout snapshot counts $152\to 4{,}026$ submissions across 22 shuttles. These record participation, not completed silicon validation; open PDKs support the implementation path [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK].](images/fig-shuttle-cost-democratization){#fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse width="80%" fig-alt="Dual-panel illustration comparing mask-set, commercial prototype, and open-shuttle entry costs across different processes and submission sizes, alongside Tiny Tapeout submission counts. The retained snapshot reaches 4,026 cumulative submissions; these are not counts of verified silicon designs."}

The educational opportunity in @fig-ch12-money-plot-tapeout-cost-collapse is access to a smaller, different experiment. A multiplexed tile on an open process cannot reproduce the capacity or physical conditions of a leading-edge commercial prototype. It can still let students bring up a fabricated design, compare measurements with predictions, and investigate discrepancies. Likewise, the submission growth in panel (b) records participation in that path; it does not establish that every submitted design was fabricated, delivered, or successfully measured. The architecture question must fit the process, area, interfaces, and observability the shuttle actually provides.

Tiny Tapeout's public run catalog and Europractice's MPW service illustrate different routes to shared fabrication [@TinyTapeoutRunCatalog; @EuropracticeMPWPrototyping]. Google's 2022 announcement of OpenMPW runs with Efabless provides an earlier example [@Google2022OpenMPW]. These programs differ in submission interfaces, process access, and implementation requirements; a team must check the terms and accepted PDK release for its planned run. The proposed extension for AI-generated macros is shared characterization infrastructure. A research shuttle could allocate isolated power-monitored rails, ring oscillators for timing characterization across voltage and temperature, and JTAG interfaces for collecting telemetry. Those features would have to be designed into the vehicle and qualified; they are not implied by booking space on a shared wafer.

A retained measurement campaign could then connect each fabricated candidate to its timing and power observations and to the models that predicted them. Yield claims would additionally need an appropriate population of devices and test conditions. This would give the community a path to calibrating surrogates against silicon rather than only against another tool. Containerized open flows improve repeatability, but do not grant commercial-tool rights or close the gap to a different foundry process.

## Consortium Governance and Benchmarking {#sec-neutral-governance}

Access to an implementation flow lets a team produce physical evidence, but comparison across teams also requires agreement on the experiment. If groups choose different RTL blocks, leave compute hours uncounted, or tune prompts against their evaluation tasks, a reported margin can mix architectural improvement with unequal budgets and selection effects, including the optimizer's curse (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). Shared tasks, reference comparators, disclosure rules, and audit procedures would address the benchmark-health risks analyzed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect.

Drawing on the governance model of MLCommons[^fn-mlcommons-c12] and MLPerf [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf], an independent Architecture Automation Working Group under an established body (such as MLCommons,[^fn-mlcommons-c12] Standard Performance Evaluation Corporation (SPEC), CHIPS Alliance, or IEEE Council on Electronic Design Automation (CEDA)) could maintain these shared rules and hear disputes over results. Separate divisions would let researchers pursue different kinds of comparison while making resource budgets explicit. Method attribution would still require the controlled comparisons and ablations developed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. Such a working group would take on three mandates:

- **Reference problem suites.** Problem suites grounded in realistic industrial constraints, spanning 3\ W mobile extended-reality (XR) spatial processing, RISC-V RV64GCV vector clusters, datacenter tensor acceleration, Compute Express Link (CXL) memory expansion, and Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) chiplet interconnect management.
- **Closed and open benchmark divisions.** A Closed Division where entrants compete under locked tool wrappers, fixed compute budgets, and identical baseline matching to compare search methods within those conditions. An Open Division could permit custom search procedures, heuristics, or proprietary surrogates while retaining the task's architectural requirements and disclosing multi-dimensional workflow costs and artifact lineage. Its results would compare complete approaches under the declared conditions.
- **Total workflow-cost accounting.** Mandatory accounting for the multi-dimensional resource vector ($C_{\text{workflow}} = \langle C_{\text{compute}}, C_{\text{license}}, C_{\text{human}} \rangle$), including graphics processing unit (GPU) compute hours, electronic design automation (EDA) license checkout minutes, and human triage time.

Together the three mandates would give research groups a common basis for comparison. A contest would also need to state which constraints its score captures and which remain untested, since a gain on the contest's metric may fail to transfer to other design tasks.[^fn-contest-benchmarks-c12]

## Grand Challenges and Design Contests {#sec-grand-challenges}

Where consortium governance would establish neutral baseline rules and cost accounting, competitive grand challenges apply that framework to focus research on unresolved architectural bottlenecks. Standardized traces and open competitions historically propelled innovations in branch prediction through Championship Branch Prediction (CBP) [@CBP2016BranchPrediction], data prefetching through Data Prefetching Championship (DPC) [@DPC2015DataPrefetching], and simulation through ChampSim [@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim], echoing the historical impact of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) Grand Challenges in autonomous vehicles [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley] and ImageNet in computer vision [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet]. EDA already runs such contests; the ISPD and ICCAD CAD contests have posed placement, routing, and timing problems on shared benchmarks for two decades, and any Architecture 2.0 challenge would be a track beside them rather than a new institution. Three such tracks are sketched below.

- **Constrained physical PPA generation.** RTL carried through a named implementation flow from a high-level specification under a declared power and thermal envelope. Entrants would be judged on the declared physical checks and intervention budget; passing the contest would not authorize tapeout.
- **Sample-efficient design-space exploration.** Microarchitectural configurations for heterogeneous workloads under a fixed simulation budget. Entrants would return candidates nondominated among those evaluated: no evaluated design is at least as good on every objective and better on one. A possible score is the fraction of evaluator-declared objective targets reached within the budget. For an energy–latency target, at least one returned candidate must meet both bounds and all feasibility checks. Targets would be fixed before submissions, and the score would not imply that the global Pareto frontier had been found.
- **Adversarial red-teaming and hardware security.** Detection of seeded timing exceptions, malicious logic, and verification loopholes in generated collateral. Timing exceptions would require constraint audits and appropriate timing analysis; SVA and BMC could expose encoded functional violations within a declared model and bound. A possible score would count correctly detected seeded defects while recording false alarms and the checks used. It would establish coverage of the declared challenge set, not the absence of every possible Trojan or timing defect.

The unsuccessful entries can remain useful after the winning score is superseded. Their retained inputs and diagnostic returns show which candidates failed under the contest's conditions, providing material for the repository proposed next.

## Public Repositories of Failed Runs {#sec-open-failed-attempts}

Discarding failed runs censors the data available to learned surrogates (@sec-data-representations-world-models). A team may treat a failed synthesis or place-and-route run as a broken experiment and remove its log. Yet an unroutable floorplan or a reported timing violation can reveal a feasibility limit that a corpus of successful designs never shows. Training only on the survivors leaves that part of the design space poorly represented.[^fn-survivorship-bias-c12] Retaining negative results gives later studies observations near those limits, provided contributors distinguish a design failure from a tool crash or configuration error. A consortium repository would need three forms of support to make these runs reusable.

- **Raw execution traces.** Complete command-line interface (CLI) logs, tool return codes, standard error (stderr) streams, and resource consumption telemetry for failed synthesis and simulation passes.
- **Root-cause taxonomy annotations.** Standardized labels categorizing failures by class: timing violations (worst negative slack $\text{WNS} < 0$), design rule checking (DRC) geometry violations, assertion counterexamples, deadlock states, unroutable congestion maps, and license timeouts.
- **Disclosure review and filtering.** Proposed sanitization pipelines could convert proprietary physical netlists into normalized graph embeddings, anonymized congestion heatmaps, and relative slack distributions, stripping absolute die coordinates, foundry cell-type names, and top-level block pinouts. These transformations would still need disclosure review because patterns across several failed runs may expose information that no single record reveals.

Publishing qualified negative data can help other teams avoid known dead ends and supply observations near the feasibility boundaries used to calibrate multi-fidelity surrogates. OpenROAD-flow-scripts already publishes a public design set with continuous integration across open PDKs; a failure repository would extend that practice from designs that build to runs that did not. Maintaining the repository would also require people to preserve tool dependencies, review annotations, and track whether old runs remain interpretable.[^fn-abandonware-c12] Contributors would need to assess what the accumulated records reveal about a product's design space, a disclosure question that remains open below.

## Ecosystem Outlook at Scale {#sec-ecosystem-outlook}

If shared foundations made closed-loop exploration economical at industry scale, problem formulation, signoff review, and cross-layer trade-offs could account for more of the remaining work. Repeated automated execution could also create demand for different EDA licensing arrangements. Lower front-end labor costs might make smaller-volume application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) viable for regional laboratories and startups, although masks, packaging, and physical validation would still have to fit the budget. These are possible consequences of the proposed infrastructure, not results established here. Their value would depend in part on whether engineers retained the diagnostic skills needed to evaluate the resulting designs.

## Curriculum and Diagnostic Competence {#sec-curriculum-certification}

The shared records, implementation paths, and failure repositories above would also change what students can practice. RTL construction and point-tool execution remain useful ways to learn hardware behavior. A curriculum for AI-native design systems must connect that experience to formulating requirements, building evaluators, orchestrating tool runs, and diagnosing generated artifacts. Four areas of competence organize that extension:

- **Specification engineering across requirement domains.** Expressing functional, timing, power, and interface requirements in forms that can be checked across the hardware–software stack.
- **Verification of generated designs.** Developing testbench architectures, property-appropriate checks, and adversarial red-teaming methodologies.
- **Search space formulation.** Defining evaluator-driven search spaces, constraint boundaries, and Pareto trade-off synthesis.
- **Heterogeneous system integration.** Integrating domain-specific accelerators across central processing unit (CPU), neural processing unit (NPU), memory, and packaging boundaries.

The educational risk is the apprenticeship gap identified in @sec-what-architect-owns. If automation removes routine debugging from a junior engineer's work, a curriculum must supply another way to learn what a timing report, waveform, or congestion map means. Otherwise the organization may assign responsibility without the experience needed to exercise it, the problem examined in @sec-sustaining-responsibility [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. Bainbridge's analysis explains why additional automation does not by itself resolve this gap [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].

::: {.callout-law title="Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation in Hardware Design"}
**The Classical Principle:** Automating routine tasks removes the operator's opportunity to practice fundamental skills, leaving the human least equipped to handle the rare, complex faults that only humans can resolve [@Bainbridge1983Ironies].

**Hardware Design Application:** A summary score can report that a candidate failed without teaching the reviewer how to distinguish a layout problem from an incorrect timing constraint. Training must include the underlying artifacts and the checks that separate those causes.

**Mitigation Strategy:** Implement shadow verification audits and diagnostic fault-injection training to restore the operator's exposure to structural debugging without reverting to routine manual drafting (@sec-law-ironies-automation in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

Two laboratory practices can provide that experience in a setting where mistakes can be investigated before fabrication. In a shadow verification audit, a student follows an automated exploration run, forms an independent hypothesis about the bottleneck the optimizer is pursuing, and audits the generated RTL and its Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) declarations. The student then compares that diagnosis with the instructor's review. The learning comes from explaining why a reported improvement survives or fails the checks, not merely observing the run complete.

In a fault-injection laboratory, instructors seed a candidate with a clock-domain crossing (CDC) synchronization defect,[^fn-cdc-metastability-c12] an unhandled finite state machine (FSM) reset state, or a silent false path in its SDC constraints. Students select the appropriate evidence for each defect: structural CDC checks for unsafe crossings, simulation or formal properties for reset behavior, and timing-constraint audits for the false path. Ordinary RTL simulation does not model analog metastability, and a passing functional trace does not validate a timing exception (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). Explaining those observation limits is part of the exercise. Shared repositories of failed runs could supply additional cases with retained inputs and instructor-checked diagnoses.

Where commercial-tool access is available, students can also compare OpenROAD and Yosys reports with corresponding industrial signoff reports, identifying which quantities and assumptions transfer. A semester-long course can follow the four parts of this book, moving from the design question through representations, methods, environments, and feedback, then into execution, transfer, evaluation, ownership, and shared infrastructure. The principles in @sec-appendix-c-design-principles provide an exit test: students should be able to apply them to a problem the course never assigned. The companion site carries the week-by-week version, since a syllabus dates faster than a chapter.

Translating classroom diagnostic practice into peer-reviewed research standards requires institutionalizing computational verification across major academic venues. Conference artifact evaluation committees at venues such as the International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO), Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS), and Design Automation Conference (DAC) could pilot an Autonomous Workflow Certified (AWC) badge grounded in computational reproducibility practice [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science].[^fn-awc-badge-c12] ACM's artifact badging already distinguishes an artifact that is available from one that has been evaluated and one whose results were reproduced; an AWC badge would extend that scheme along the dimensions this book has argued matter for a workflow, from replay under declared execution conditions, through signed lineage and total-cost accounting, to surrogate calibration against signoff checks and physical closure on an open manufacturable kit.

The proposed badge would need to name exactly what reviewers checked. Computational repeatability and lineage could be assessed for a simulator study; surrogate calibration would require a declared reference; an implementation study could additionally be reviewed for physical closure in a named open flow. These are different scopes, and a badge should not imply that each artifact passed all of them. Even open-flow physical closure would not establish commercial foundry signoff, electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection, process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) yield qualification, or packaging thermo-mechanical qualification. Nor would computational review substitute for measurements on fabricated silicon or authorize commercial tapeout. Publishing the reviewed scope would let readers use the badge as evidence of specific checks rather than as a general certificate of architectural correctness.

[^fn-awc-badge-c12]: **Autonomous Workflow Certified (AWC) badge**: A proposed designation in this chapter, extending computational reproducibility principles to an explicitly scoped review of an automated design workflow. The cited work motivates reproducibility practice; it does not establish this badge [@Stodden2010ReproducibleResearch; @StoddenEtAl2016Science].

## Open Questions {#sec-ecosystem-open-questions}

The questions that close each chapter state what its argument could not settle. Here the unresolved issues concern arrangements between teams: how shared infrastructure could support comparisons while preserving access, independence, and confidentiality.

- **When do architectural rankings from open predictive PDKs survive commercial signoff?** A predictive kit such as ASAP7 supports comparisons within its modeled process, but those rankings do not establish how candidates compare under a commercial foundry's rules and models. The shared infrastructure would need a way to discover which constraints cause rankings to change without requiring every contributor to obtain the same restricted access. The unresolved issue is how matched open and commercial evaluations could establish useful transfer limits while respecting the foundry's disclosure restrictions.

- **How can a neutral evaluation consortium remain independent when its rulings disqualify member products?** Members may supply both the funding and the expertise needed to evaluate a result, yet face a commercial loss when an audit rejects it. Publishing rules makes the decision inspectable, but does not settle how the consortium sustains its reviewers, funding, and enforcement under that pressure. Possible arrangements include public support, audits distributed among competing groups, or separation between benchmark authors and tool vendors; their ability to preserve both technical competence and independence would need to be tested.

- **How much of a product's design space does a corpus of its failed runs reveal?** Removing coordinates, cell names, and pinouts does not establish that disclosure is safe. A failure corpus also records which floorplans a team tried and abandoned, at what congestion and under what slack. The combination may reveal information absent from individual records. The proposed repository therefore needs an evaluation of reconstruction risk and of whether contribution pooling, bounded release under a privacy budget, or delayed release after product launch would reduce that risk to a level contributors can accept.

- **Who can sustain historical reference tasks and reruns across institutions?** The benchmark-renewal methods discussed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect depend on continued access to reference tasks, earlier systems, and the tools needed to rerun them. A distributed archive could outlast a single laboratory, but preserving a package does not preserve its licenses, services, or compatible execution environment. The open issue is which shared custody and access arrangements could keep historical comparisons usable as institutions and vendors change, and how to state the limits when some dependencies can no longer be recovered.

- **How can independent groups test the integrity of a consortium's reference baselines?** Shared reference flows and audit scripts can drift or favor some candidates, so agreement to use them does not establish that they remain credible comparators. Cryptographically signed lineage can reveal which artifacts were used; it cannot establish that the comparator was configured competently or given a fair budget. Independent reruns and adversarial re-audits could challenge that technical basis, but the community still needs to determine what access and coverage make such challenges effective.

## Next Steps: Immediate Local Actions {#sec-ecosystem-coda}

The fabrication-access story that opens this chapter joins two kinds of work: methods that a team can learn and shared services that let it test what it builds. The proposed ecosystem needs the same connection. A record format has value when another laboratory can interpret it; a reference flow has value when researchers can reach the checks their claims require. Individual teams can begin preparing those contributions while the broader agreements are still being formed.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Prepare records for another reader.** Retain units, versions, status meanings, costs, and dependencies so a collaborator can interpret a run without relying on its author's memory.
- **Keep failures with their context.** Preserve inputs and diagnostic returns, distinguish tool failures from rejected designs, and review disclosure risks before contributing records to a shared repository.
- **Name the implementation path.** Identify which modeled checks your open flow supports and what additional process access or fabricated measurements a broader claim would require.
- **Make a comparison reusable.** Version the task, comparator, checks, and workflow costs together so another group can attempt the same comparison and report where it differs.
- **Teach diagnosis through retained artifacts.** Use shadow audits and fault-injection exercises to let students explain failures, select checks, and recognize what those checks cannot observe.
:::

The questions across this book are food for thought, not a complete research agenda. They leave room for a student to contribute before the discipline has settled these arrangements. A new study may reveal that two tools disagree about a status, that a shared benchmark omits a relevant constraint, or that an apparently anonymous failure record exposes too much. State your own question, identify the observation that could answer it, and retain what the study leaves unresolved. Carry that habit to the next workload, tool, or implementation process, including those this lecture could not anticipate.




[^fn-mlcommons-c12]: **MLCommons / CHIPS Alliance**: Existing consortia that define standardized benchmarks (like MLPerf) or open-source hardware standards. An Architecture Automation Working Group would build directly on their governance models.

[^fn-ir-drop-c12]: **IR Drop**: The voltage decrease that occurs when current (I) flows through the resistance (R) of the power distribution network, potentially causing transistors to switch slower or fail entirely.

[^fn-bmc-c12]: **Bounded model checking (BMC)**: A formal verification technique that searches executions of a circuit model up to a finite bound for counterexamples to an encoded property. Passing that bound alone does not establish unbounded correctness. For a finite-state model, a sufficiently large bound can establish the property if a completeness threshold for that model and property has been justified.

[^fn-cdc-metastability-c12]: **CDC Metastability**: An unpredictable physical state that occurs when a signal transitions between two asynchronous clock domains exactly as the receiving flip-flop is capturing data, leading to settling delays that digital simulation models typically miss.
[^fn-rc-parasitics-c12]: **RC Parasitics / Delays**: The signal propagation delay caused by the inherent resistance (R) and capacitance (C) of the microscopic metal wires connecting transistors on a chip.
[^fn-abandonware-c12]: **Software degradation in academic infrastructure**: Academic infrastructure decay mirrors open-source software degradation, where unmaintained repositories rapidly become unusable without active consortium stewardship and containerized CI/CD integration.
[^fn-pdk-lockin-c12]: **Proprietary isolation in EDA**: NDA-enforced PDK restrictions create proprietary silos, impeding scientific progress by preventing independent audit and verification of claimed physical design improvements.
[^fn-contest-benchmarks-c12]: **Overfitting in competitive benchmarks**: Uncalibrated contest metrics suffer from the benchmark over-optimization trap observed in machine learning, where systems overfit to specific contest artifacts while degrading on general engineering tasks.
[^fn-survivorship-bias-c12]: **Survivorship bias in training data**: Training surrogate models only on valid, timing-closed designs blinds optimizers to physical infeasibility bounds, causing generative search to repeatedly propose unroutable layouts.
